passages.t: The love of youth, and two evils
passages.happening:
God sends Jeremiah to speak in Jerusalem's hearing. God remembers ‘the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness, in a land not sown’ (verse 2). Israel was holy to the LORD, the firstfruits of his harvest (verse 3).

‘What fault did your fathers find in Me that they strayed so far from Me, and followed worthless idols, and became worthless themselves?’ (verse 5). They never asked where the LORD was who brought them out of Egypt and through the wilderness (verse 6). He brought them into a fertile land, and they defiled it (verse 7). The priests did not ask for him, the experts in the law did not know him, the leaders rebelled, and the prophets prophesied by Baal (verse 8).

So God brings a case against them (verse 9). They can search from Cyprus to Kedar and find no nation that has changed its gods, ‘though they are no gods at all’ (verse 11). ‘For My people have committed two evils: They have forsaken Me, the fountain of living water, and they have dug their own cisterns’ (verse 13), cisterns that are broken and cannot hold water.
passages.hearers:
Many scholars think this chapter keeps some of Jeremiah's earliest preaching, from Josiah's reign. It is set out like a lawsuit. God remembers the early years, then lays out his charge, calls heaven as witness, and gives his verdict.

Water shaped life in Judah's hill country. A spring was called living water because it flowed, and it was the best water there was. Where there was no spring, people cut cisterns into the limestone and plastered them to catch winter rain. A cracked cistern leaked, and whatever water stayed went stale. To leave a spring for a cistern was foolish. To dig cisterns that could not even hold water was absurd.

People who follow worthless things become worthless themselves. Cyprus lay to the west and Kedar to the east in the Arabian desert; search the whole world, east and west, and nothing like this will be found.
passages.later: Hosea speaks of the same early love in the wilderness: ‘There she will respond as she did in the days of her youth’ (Hosea 2:15). A psalm says of idols, ‘Those who make them become like them’ (Psalm 115:8).
passages.asks: God asks what fault the people found in him. Ask what you have reached for instead of God, and whether it holds water. And ask what it would mean to come back to the spring rather than dig another cistern.

passages.t: Plundered by the powers they trusted
passages.happening:
‘Is Israel a slave? Was he born into slavery? Why then has he become prey?’ (verse 14). Lions have roared over him, and his cities lie in ruins (verse 15). The men of Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved his head (verse 16). ‘Have you not brought this on yourself by forsaking the LORD your God when He led you in the way?’ (verse 17).

What will they gain by going to Egypt to drink the Nile, or to Assyria to drink the Euphrates (verse 18)? ‘Your own evil will discipline you; your own apostasies will reprimand you’ (verse 19).

Long ago they broke the yoke and refused to serve. On every high hill and under every green tree they gave themselves to other gods (verse 20). God planted them as a choice vine, and they became a wild one (verse 21). No soap can wash out the stain (verse 22). They say they are not defiled, but they are like a young camel running here and there, or a wild donkey in heat (verses 23 and 24). They say a tree is their father and a stone their mother, yet in trouble they beg God to rise and save them. The gods they made are as many as their cities, so let those gods save them (verses 27 and 28).
passages.hearers:
Judah's kings had long swung between the two great powers. Ahaz had appealed to Assyria, and later kings looked to Egypt. Verse 18 assumes Assyria is still worth courting, which fits the years before its collapse around 609 BC.

Memphis was the old capital of Lower Egypt, and Tahpanhes a frontier fortress in the eastern Nile Delta. A shaved head was a picture of humiliation.

The worship condemned here is Canaanite religion, centered on Baal, the storm god believed to send rain and fertility. Shrines stood on high hills and under green trees, with wooden poles and standing stones. The prophet's pictures of an animal in heat are deliberately crude. They show a people driven by appetite, running after gods who could not help.
passages.later: Isaiah gave the same warning about Egypt: ‘They set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice’ (Isaiah 30:2). A psalm sings of the vine God brought out of Egypt (Psalm 80:8).
passages.hard:
Why does the chapter picture God's people as a prostitute and an animal in heat?

The prophets described the covenant as a marriage, so turning to other gods was called unfaithfulness. The worship at the hill shrines may have included sexual rites, so the language is partly literal, and its crudeness is meant to shock a people who thought they were innocent. The picture is of a whole people, men and women alike, kings and priests and prophets among them (verse 26).

This is a prophetic picture of a city and a covenant. It gives no warrant for any man to shame or harm any woman.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people ran to Egypt and Assyria instead of God, and both failed them. Ask where you run for help first, and whether it has ever failed you. And ask what stain you have tried to scrub out yourself that only God can remove.

passages.t: Claiming innocence, and disappointed by Egypt
passages.happening:
‘Why do you bring a case against Me? You have all rebelled against Me’ (verse 29). God struck their children, and they would not learn. Their own sword devoured their prophets (verse 30).

‘Have I been a wilderness to Israel or a land of dense darkness?’ (verse 31). Why do they say they are free to roam and will come to him no more? ‘Does a maiden forget her jewelry or a bride her wedding sash? Yet My people have forgotten Me for days without number’ (verse 32).

Their skirts are stained with the blood of the innocent poor (verse 34). Yet they say they are innocent and that God's anger will turn away. God will judge them because they say they have not sinned (verse 35). ‘You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria’ (verse 36). They will go out with their hands on their heads, because the LORD has rejected those they trust (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
The lawsuit turns around. The people have been bringing a case against God, complaining about what has happened to them. God answers that they are the ones who rebelled.

The bride and her wedding sash is a gentle picture set among hard ones. No bride forgets what she wears on her wedding day. God's people have forgotten him for days without number.

Verse 34 adds injustice to idolatry. The blood of the innocent poor is on their clothes, though the poor had done nothing to deserve it. The covenant was broken both in worship and in the way the poor were treated.

Hands on the head was a sign of grief and shame, like a captive led away.
passages.later: John writes, ‘If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves’ (1 John 1:8). Ezekiel says the people's trust in Egypt was ‘a staff of reeds’ (Ezekiel 29:6).
passages.asks: The people insisted they had not sinned, and that was the sin God judged. Ask whether there is something you insist you are innocent of. And ask what God might say to you about how the poor are treated around you.
